title: Vector equations of planes
summary: A plane is a flat surface that goes on for ever. You can fix it by one point and two directions in it, or by one point and a [[normal-vector|normal]] that sticks straight out of it. Each way gives an equation, and exam questions expect you to move freely between all three forms.

goals.text: Write a vector equation $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b} + \mu\boldsymbol{c}$ of a plane from a point and two directions, or from three points.
Write the normal form $\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = \boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$, using the [[vector-product|vector product]] to find a [[normal-vector|normal]] when you need one.
Write and read the Cartesian equation $ax + by + cz = d$, and test whether a point lies on a plane.
Convert a plane from any one of the three forms to the others.

synonyms: r = a + lambda b + mu c
r dot n = a dot n

before.prompt: Which vector is a direction vector of the line through $\mathrm{M}(2, 5, -1)$ and $\mathrm{N}(-1, 3, 4)$?
before.hint: A direction comes from subtracting the coordinates of one point from the other's.
before.explain: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{MN}} = \begin{pmatrix}-1 - 2\\3 - 5\\4 - (-1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-3\\-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$. The vector $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ is the position vector of N, not a direction. Revise it in {{lesson:3.14}}.

before.hint: Two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is $0$.
before.explain: $\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix} = 3 - 4 + 1 = 0$. The vector $\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ is parallel to it, not perpendicular. Revise it in {{lesson:3.13}}.

$\begin{pmatrix}1(3) - 0(-1)\\0(1) - 2(3)\\2(-1) - 1(1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\\-3\end{pmatrix}$. $\begin{pmatrix}-3\\6\\3\end{pmatrix}$ is the product taken in the other order. Revise it in {{lesson:3.16}}.

sections.heading: A plane from a point and two directions

blocks.text: A line needs one point and one direction. On a tabletop you can slide left and right, and also forwards and back. So a plane needs one point and two directions.
The two directions must not be [[parallel-vectors|parallel]], or you could only move along one line.

blocks.statement: The plane through the point with position vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ that contains the non-parallel vectors $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ has vector equation $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b} + \mu\boldsymbol{c}$, where $\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$.
blocks.plain: Start at a known point, then move any amount along each of two directions that lie in the plane.

blocks.text: $\boldsymbol{a}$ is the [[position-vector|position vector]] of a known point A on the plane. $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ are two directions in the plane. $\lambda$ (lambda) and $\mu$ (mu) are real numbers you choose.
Each pair of values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ gives one point, and $\boldsymbol{r}$ is its position vector. As $\lambda$ and $\mu$ take every real value, the points fill the whole plane.

blocks.alt: A plane drawn as a tilted parallelogram, with the origin O below it. Vector a runs from O to the point A on the plane. Arrows b and c point from A along the plane in different directions. A dashed path goes two steps along b, then one along c, to the point R. A dashed vector r runs from O to R.
blocks.caption: Here $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = 1$: two steps of $\boldsymbol{b}$, then one step of $\boldsymbol{c}$, reach R.

blocks.text: This is the [[vector-equation-of-a-plane|vector equation]] of the plane, and it is in the booklet. It is the vector equation of a line from {{lesson:3.14}} with one more direction. Always start it with $\boldsymbol{r} =$.
A plane has many vector equations. Any point on it can be $\boldsymbol{a}$. Any two non-parallel directions in it can be $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$.
Three points A, B and C that are not on one line fix exactly one plane. Start at A. Use the displacements from A to the other two points as the directions.

blocks.question: The plane $\Pi$ passes through $\mathrm{A}(3, -1, 2)$ and contains the directions $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Write down a vector equation of $\Pi$. Find the point on $\Pi$ given by $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = -3$.
steps: Use the point as $\boldsymbol{a}$ and the two directions as $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$: $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
The directions are not parallel, since their first components are $1$ and $0$.
Substitute $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = -3$: $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix} + 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix} - 3\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
Add component by component: $\begin{pmatrix}3 + 2 + 0\\-1 + 0 - 3\\2 + 4 + 3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}5\\-4\\9\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.question: Find a vector equation of the plane through $\mathrm{D}(1, 2, -1)$, $\mathrm{E}(4, 0, 1)$ and $\mathrm{F}(2, 5, 0)$.
steps: Find two directions from D: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DE}} = \begin{pmatrix}4 - 1\\0 - 2\\1 - (-1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DF}} = \begin{pmatrix}2 - 1\\5 - 2\\0 - (-1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
Check they are not parallel. If $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DE}} = k\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DF}}$, the $x$-components give $k = 3$, but $3 \times 3 \ne -2$. So D, E and F are not on one line.
Start at D and use the two displacements as the directions.

blocks.text: Using a position vector as a direction. $\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ says where E is. It is a direction in the plane only if the plane passes through the origin. Use a displacement such as $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DE}}$.

blocks.question: The point $\mathrm{S}(6, -5, k)$ lies on the plane through D, E and F above. Find $k$.
steps: Write the general point of the plane: $x = 1 + 3\lambda + \mu$, $y = 2 - 2\lambda + 3\mu$ and $z = -1 + 2\lambda + \mu$.
Use the two components without $k$: $1 + 3\lambda + \mu = 6$ and $2 - 2\lambda + 3\mu = -5$. So $3\lambda + \mu = 5$ and $-2\lambda + 3\mu = -7$.
From the first, $\mu = 5 - 3\lambda$. Substitute: $-2\lambda + 15 - 9\lambda = -7$, so $-11\lambda = -22$ and $\lambda = 2$. Then $\mu = 5 - 6 = -1$.
Put both values into the $z$-component: $k = -1 + 2(2) + (-1) = 2$.
Check: $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = -1$ give $x = 6$ and $y = -5$, as required.

blocks.prompt: Which is a vector equation of the plane through $\mathrm{A}(2, 0, -3)$, $\mathrm{B}(5, 1, -1)$ and $\mathrm{C}(0, 4, -2)$?
blocks.hint: Find $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}}$, and check they are not parallel.
blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}$, which are not parallel. $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{BA}}$ is parallel to $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$, and $(3, 1, 2)$ is not on the plane.

blocks.prompt: The line $L: \boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix} + t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and the point $\mathrm{G}(3, 1, 4)$ lie in the plane $\Pi$. Which is a vector equation of $\Pi$?
blocks.hint: The line gives one point and one direction. For a second direction, go from a point on $L$ to G.
blocks.explain: From $(1, -2, 0)$ on $L$ to G is $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}$, not parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, and G can be the starting point. $\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}$ is a position vector, and $\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ is parallel to the line.

blocks.text: Stand a pencil upright on a table. It is at right angles to every line you could draw on the table. A vector along the pencil is a [[normal-vector|normal]] to the plane of the table.

blocks.statement: A normal to a plane is a non-zero vector $\boldsymbol{n}$ that is perpendicular to every vector lying in the plane.
blocks.plain: It points straight out of the plane.

blocks.text: One point A and a normal $\boldsymbol{n}$ fix a plane. Any non-zero multiple of $\boldsymbol{n}$ is also a normal, so scale it to keep the numbers small.

blocks.alt: A plane drawn as a tilted parallelogram. From the point A on it, an arrow n points straight out of the plane. An arrow from A to another point R lies in the plane, and a small square at A marks the right angle between the two arrows.
blocks.caption: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AR}} = \boldsymbol{r} - \boldsymbol{a}$ lies in the plane, so it is perpendicular to $\boldsymbol{n}$.

blocks.text: Take any point R on the plane, with position vector $\boldsymbol{r}$. The vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AR}} = \boldsymbol{r} - \boldsymbol{a}$ lies in the plane. So it is perpendicular to $\boldsymbol{n}$, and its [[scalar-product|scalar product]] with $\boldsymbol{n}$ is $0$.
Expand the bracket and move $\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$ to the right-hand side. This gives the normal form of the plane, which is in the booklet.

The right-hand side $\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$ is a number, so work it out. A point lies on the plane exactly when the scalar product of its position vector with $\boldsymbol{n}$ gives that same number.

blocks.question: Find an equation of the plane through $\mathrm{A}(2, -3, 1)$ with normal $\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, in the form $\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = \boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$. Determine whether $\mathrm{B}(0, 5, 1)$ lies on the plane.
steps: Find the number on the right: $\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix} = 8 - 3 - 2 = 3$.
So the plane is $\boldsymbol{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix} = 3$.
Test B: $\begin{pmatrix}0\\5\\1\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix} = 0 + 5 - 2 = 3$. This equals the right-hand side, so B lies on the plane.

Check: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix} = -8 + 8 + 0 = 0$, so $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ lies in the plane.

blocks.text: Given three points instead of a normal, you need a vector perpendicular to two directions in the plane. The [[vector-product|vector product]] $\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c}$ from {{lesson:3.16}} gives one. It is in the booklet:

blocks.tex: \boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix} v_{2}w_{3} - v_{3}w_{2} \\ v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3} \\ v_{1}w_{2} - v_{2}w_{1} \end{pmatrix}

blocks.question: Find an equation of the plane through $\mathrm{D}(1, 2, -1)$, $\mathrm{E}(4, 0, 1)$ and $\mathrm{F}(2, 5, 0)$ in the form $\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = \boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$.
steps: Two directions in the plane, as before: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DE}} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DF}} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

Take their vector product: $\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}(-2)(1) - (2)(3)\\(2)(1) - (3)(1)\\(3)(3) - (-2)(1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-8\\-1\\11\end{pmatrix}$.
Check the normal against both directions: $3(-8) + (-2)(-1) + 2(11) = 0$ and $1(-8) + 3(-1) + 1(11) = 0$.
Multiply by $-1$ to tidy the signs: $\boldsymbol{n} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\1\\-11\end{pmatrix}$ is also a normal.
Use D for $\boldsymbol{a}$: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}8\\1\\-11\end{pmatrix} = 8 + 2 + 11 = 21$.
Check with E: $8(4) + 1(0) - 11(1) = 21$, the same number.

blocks.text: Getting the middle entry of your vector product wrong. It is $v_3w_1 - v_1w_3$, the opposite way round to the other two. Check that your normal has scalar product $0$ with both directions.

blocks.prompt: The plane through $(4, -1, 2)$ with normal $\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ has equation $\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix} = d$. Find $d$.

The plane $\Pi$ contains $\mathrm{B}(0, 3, -1)$. It is at right angles to the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\2\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\5\end{pmatrix}$. Which is an equation of $\Pi$?
blocks.hint: A line perpendicular to a plane runs along its normal. Which point is on $\Pi$?
blocks.explain: The line's direction $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\5\end{pmatrix}$ is a normal. Using B, the right-hand side is $0(2) + 3(-1) + (-1)(5) = -8$. The value $16$ uses the line's point, which is not on $\Pi$.

blocks.text: In the normal form, write $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{n} = \begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix}$. The scalar product on the left becomes $ax + by + cz$. Call the number on the right $d$.

This is the [[cartesian-equation-of-a-plane|Cartesian equation]] of the plane, and it is in the booklet. Its coefficients give a [[normal-vector|normal]] at once: $ax + by + cz = d$ has normal $\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix}$.
Before you read off the normal, collect $x$, $y$ and $z$ on the left. A missing letter has coefficient $0$. For example, $x - 2z = 4$ has normal $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.
To test a point, substitute its coordinates. It lies on the plane only if you get $d$. A plane through the origin has $d = 0$.

blocks.question: Find the Cartesian equation of the plane through $(-1, 4, 2)$ with normal $\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: The normal gives the left-hand side: $3x - 2y + 5z = d$.
Substitute the point to find $d$: $3(-1) - 2(4) + 5(2) = -3 - 8 + 10 = -1$.
Check by the normal form: $d = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\2\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\5\end{pmatrix} = -1$ too.

blocks.text: Parallel planes have parallel normals. So a plane parallel to $ax + by + cz = d$ keeps the left-hand side and changes only $d$.

blocks.question: The plane $\Pi_1$ has equation $2x - 5y + z = 7$. Find the Cartesian equation of the plane $\Pi_2$ through $(3, 1, -4)$ that is parallel to $\Pi_1$.
steps: Read the normal of $\Pi_1$ from its coefficients: $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
$\Pi_2$ is parallel, so it has the same normal: $2x - 5y + z = d$.
Substitute the point: $d = 2(3) - 5(1) + (-4) = 6 - 5 - 4 = -3$.
Since $-3 \ne 7$, $\Pi_2$ is not $\Pi_1$ itself.

blocks.text: Reading the normal from an untidy equation. A term on the right-hand side changes sign when you move it to the left, so collect $x$, $y$ and $z$ first.

blocks.prompt: Which vector is a normal to the plane $4y - x = 2z + 3$?
blocks.hint: Move $2z$ to the left-hand side first, then read the coefficients of $x$, $y$ and $z$ in that order.
blocks.explain: Rearranged, the plane is $-x + 4y - 2z = 3$, so a normal is $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}$. $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}$ forgets that $2z$ changes sign.

blocks.prompt: The point $(k, 2, -1)$ lies on the plane $5x - 3y + 2z = 4$. Find $k$.
blocks.hint: Substitute the coordinates and solve for $k$.

blocks.text: From vector form to [[cartesian-equation-of-a-plane|Cartesian form]]: $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ lie in the plane, so their [[vector-product|vector product]] $\boldsymbol{n} = \boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c}$ is a [[normal-vector|normal]]. Then $d = \boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$.

blocks.question: Find the Cartesian equation of the plane $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: Find a normal: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}(2)(1) - (0)(-1)\\(0)(3) - (1)(1)\\(1)(-1) - (2)(3)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-7\end{pmatrix}$.
Check: $2 - 2 + 0 = 0$ and $6 + 1 - 7 = 0$, so the normal is perpendicular to both directions.
So the plane is $2x - y - 7z = d$. Substitute the point $(2, 0, -1)$: $d = 4 - 0 + 7 = 11$.
Check with $\lambda = \mu = 1$, which gives the point $(6, 1, 0)$: $12 - 1 - 0 = 11$.

blocks.text: From Cartesian to vector form, let two coordinates be the parameters, such as $y = \lambda$ and $z = \mu$. Then solve the equation for the third coordinate.

blocks.question: Find a vector equation of the plane $x - 2y + 3z = 6$.
steps: Let $y = \lambda$ and $z = \mu$. Then $x = 6 + 2\lambda - 3\mu$.
Write the general point as one vector: $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}6 + 2\lambda - 3\mu\\\lambda\\\mu\end{pmatrix}$.
Split it into the constant part, the $\lambda$ part and the $\mu$ part: $\begin{pmatrix}6\\0\\0\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
Check each direction against the normal $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}$: $2 - 2 + 0 = 0$ and $-3 + 0 + 3 = 0$. The point $(6, 0, 0)$ gives $6 = 6$.

blocks.prompt: Which is the Cartesian equation of the plane $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$?
blocks.hint: Find the vector product of the two directions, then substitute the point.
blocks.explain: $\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\\2\end{pmatrix}$, so a normal is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-5\\-2\end{pmatrix}$. Then $d = 1 + 5 - 6 = 0$: this plane passes through the origin. $-x - 5y + 2z = 10$ comes from a sign slip in the middle component.

blocks.prompt: Which is a vector equation of the plane $2x - y + z = 4$?
blocks.hint: Let $x = \lambda$ and $z = \mu$, and solve for $y$. Then check each direction against the normal.
blocks.explain: $y = 2\lambda + \mu - 4$, so the point is $(0, -4, 0)$ and the directions are $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ is the normal, and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel.

blocks.text: On Paper 2 your calculator gives another route from three points. If the plane misses the origin, $d \ne 0$, so dividing by $d$ gives $ax + by + cz = 1$ for new values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
Each point gives one linear equation in $a$, $b$ and $c$, and the calculator solves the three.

blocks.question: Use your calculator to find the Cartesian equation of the plane through $\mathrm{A}(1, 2, 2)$, $\mathrm{B}(5, 0, 2)$ and $\mathrm{C}(-2, 1, 4)$. Give the equation with integer coefficients.
steps: Write the plane as $ax + by + cz = 1$, assuming it misses the origin.
Substitute each point and write the system down: $a + 2b + 2c = 1$, $5a + 2c = 1$ and $-2a + b + 4c = 1$. This line earns the method mark.
The calculator gives $a = 0.1$, $b = 0.2$ and $c = 0.25$. So the plane is $0.1x + 0.2y + 0.25z = 1$.
Multiply by $20$ to clear the decimals: $2x + 4y + 5z = 20$.

Check with the vector product: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-4\\-8\\-10\end{pmatrix}$, a multiple of $\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\5\end{pmatrix}$.

ti84: SIMULT EQN SOLVER, 3 equations, 3 unknowns (check on your model)
SOLVE, read X1 = 0.1, X2 = 0.2, X3 = 0.25 as a, b, c
nspire: Calculator page, Menu, Algebra, Solve System of Linear Equations
Number of equations 3, variables a,b,c, OK (check on your model)
casio: Number of unknowns: 3 (check on your model)
SOLVE (check on your model), read 0.1, 0.2 and 0.25 as a, b and c

blocks.text: If the calculator finds no single solution, the plane may pass through the origin. Use the vector product method instead.

Vector form: $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b} + \mu\boldsymbol{c}$, with $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ non-parallel directions in the plane. Always start with $\boldsymbol{r} =$.
Through three points A, B and C, use $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}}$ as the directions, never a position vector.
Normal form: $\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = \boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$, where $\boldsymbol{n}$ is perpendicular to the plane. Work out $\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$ as a number.
Cartesian form: $ax + by + cz = d$. The coefficients give a normal $\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix}$, and $d$ comes from substituting a point.

Vector form to Cartesian: $\boldsymbol{n} = \boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c}$, then $d = \boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}$. Check that $\boldsymbol{n}$ has scalar product $0$ with $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$.
Cartesian to vector form: set two coordinates equal to $\lambda$ and $\mu$, then solve for the third.
Parallel planes share a normal: the same left-hand side with a different $d$.

mistakes: Leaving out $\boldsymbol{r} =$. Without it you have an expression, not the equation of a plane.
Using a position vector as a direction in the plane. Directions come from the difference of two points, such as $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$.
Getting the middle component of the vector product wrong. It is $v_3w_1 - v_1w_3$. Check that your normal has scalar product $0$ with both directions.
Using the normal as a direction in the plane. It points out of the plane, so it can never be $\boldsymbol{b}$ or $\boldsymbol{c}$.
Reading the normal from an untidy equation. Collect $x$, $y$ and $z$ on the left first: $3x = 2y - z + 1$ has normal $\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
Choosing two parallel directions, such as $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{BA}}$. They only describe a line, so check that neither direction is a multiple of the other.
examTips: "Write down" a vector equation of a plane needs no working, but it must start with $\boldsymbol{r} =$. Any point on the plane and any two non-parallel directions in it earn the marks.
"Find the Cartesian equation": show the vector product for the normal, then the substitution for $d$.
"Show that" a plane has a given equation: work forwards from the given points or directions, and make your last line the given equation.
On Paper 1, keep every value exact and scale a normal to clear fractions. On Paper 2, write down the equations you put into the calculator.
